html:
Named world fairytale premises

Brief original premise notes for the versions collected by Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm: in Rapunzel, a young woman is kept in a forest tower with a high window but no door or stairs. That setting limits ordinary visits. In Little Red-Cap, the child travels through a wood to her grandmother and is drawn away from the path by flowers. The wooded route affects the journey. Discuss story choices; do not act out climbing, leaving safe paths or meeting strangers. Compare who, where and the connection, rather than merely naming a tower or forest.

html:
Two complete original stories and response cards

Story A: “Milo the mouse arrived in a new classroom. He could not find the book box. Tessa the turtle showed him the shelf. Later Milo saved Tessa a seat. They read together.” Story B: “On the moon, Pip the fox guarded a silver garden. A little robot asked for one seed. Pip hid the seed bag. Then Pip noticed the robot’s empty pot. Pip shared a seed, and together they planted it.” Feature cards: mouse helps turtle / new classroom / fox hides seeds then shares / silver moon garden. Sort character behaviour and setting; identify a problem or change when one is present. Reader 1: “I prefer A because the helpful characters make the new classroom feel welcoming.” Reader 2: “I prefer B because its unusual moon garden makes me curious.” Both preferences are valid and grounded in details. Discuss how you feel about Pip’s hiding and sharing; one action does not prove every animal behaves that way.

Complete original character and setting comparisons

Character A: “Rae was carrying the bags. ‘You can rest now,’ Rae whispered to the tired visitor.” Character B: “Rae was dragging the bags. ‘Hurry up!’ Rae snapped at the tired visitor.” Compare was carrying / was dragging and whispered / snapped: these action and dialogue choices can suggest different attitudes in this moment. They do not prove Rae’s permanent personality. Setting A: “Soft rain tapped the window. New leaves shone on the tree.” Setting B: “Hard rain hammered the window. Bare branches shook in the wind.” Compare sound and plant clues, then explain the different impression. These are two invented seasonal scenes; do not infer a named season everywhere in Australia from one clue. Rewrite one line to change its mood, and say which words you changed.

A complete original rhyme and a home-language comparison

Original rhyme: “Little boat beside the shore, / Gentle waves come back once more. / Tap, tap, wait, then tap again; / Hear the drops of evening rain.” Say it aloud: shore/more is one rhyming pair. Again/rain may rhyme in some pronunciations and not others; do not mark an accent wrong. The returning tap words create a pattern. Compare the four pulse spans supplied here, then reproduce them and replace one word while retaining their timing. Adult or family may choose a short permitted rhyme, chant or song in a home language, model its actual pronunciation and meaning, and point out a repeated sound or word. Name the language and source, accept listening or accessible participation, and do not guess a translation or require a family to perform.

html:
A complete original story, adaptation and edit targets

Original story: “Nell carried a seed to the garden. Rain began before Nell could plant it. Nell waited under a shelter. When the rain stopped, Nell planted the seed.” Four panels: character and goal / rain problem / waiting response / planting ending. Adapted version: “A robot carried a seed across a moon garden. Its wheel stuck in soft dust. ‘Please help me roll free,’ it called. A friend laid a board across the dust, and the robot reached the planting bed.” This changes character, place, obstacle, response and speech while retaining a goal–difficulty–response–ending structure. Sentence edit: “The robot called” can become “The robot with a long silver arm called from the garden gate.” The added phrases describe which robot and where it calls; these are new fictional details. Out-of-order draft: “Nell planted the seed. The rain stopped. Nell waited under a shelter.” Move the planting after the rain stops, then reread the whole draft. Make your own drawing, words or performance, and show one real edit; naming an edit is not the same as doing it. Digital option with an adult: use an approved drawing or presentation tool to make two original screens titled Problem and Ending. Add your own robot drawings and captions showing the stuck wheel and a coherent rescue. Reorder the screens if needed, change one caption or event to make the connection clearer, then reread the actual revised version. No online sharing is needed.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Three complete original texts about frog growth

Poem: “A tiny tadpole flicks its tail. / Small legs grow beside the trail. / A young frog rests beside the pool; / The shaded water feels so cool.” Imagined narrative: “Tilly watched a tadpole in the class record. In the next drawing it had legs. Later she drew a young frog beside the pond. ‘It has changed!’ she said.” Information: “A frog life cycle includes eggs, tadpoles, froglets and adults. Tadpoles hatch from eggs. As they develop, legs grow and their bodies change.” The information gives a broader stage sequence; the poem uses line breaks and a sound pattern, and the narrative follows Tilly’s noticing over time. They all concern frog growth; the poem and story do not include every life stage. Choose two of these texts first and name them A and B. Sort details actually present into both chosen texts / only text A / only text B. Do not add a scientific detail merely because you know it from elsewhere.

Actual exchange and paper-task directions

Idea card: “The reading corner needs a lamp so we can see the books.” First paraphrase that idea without changing it. Then ask a relevant question such as where the lamp would go, or add a reason or suggestion. Opinion cards: “I prefer a quiet reading game because I can hear the story.” “I prefer a word hunt because I enjoy finding clues.” Respond with a connected agreement or respectful alternative, not a criticism of the person. Paper task: draw a square; put a small circle inside it; draw a star above the square. Give or receive those directions in order, check the listener’s drawing, and repair “Put it there” by naming the shape and position. Discuss one statement, one opinion and one instruction. Partners swap roles. Observe actual contributions and clarification; eye contact, accent and one particular posture are not required evidence.

Complete purpose, audience, sign and advertisement texts

Imaginative: “At midnight a tiny moon boat landed on the library roof. The books whispered, ‘Take us to the stars!’” Informative: “Our library opens at nine. Books are grouped by topic. Ask at the desk if you need help.” Persuasive advertisement: “Families, join our Saturday library story club. Share a story together and discover a new favourite book!” Sign A: “Library visitors: return borrowed books in this box.” Sign B: “Story club meets here at ten.” Ask what each text helps a reader know, imagine or do, and who the words address. A sign can direct or inform, and a poster can advertise or tell facts. Form alone does not determine purpose. Another valid purpose or audience is welcome when supported by the full supplied text.

html:
Actual reading passage and controlled repair

Passage: “After lunch, the children carried a seed box to the garden. A small bird landed on the fence. The children planted six seeds and went back inside.” Before independent reading, the adult may explain the task but should not read the target words or passage to the learner. Practise a different model first. Word cards: planted = plant + ed; seedlings = seed + ling + s; lunchbox = lunch + box. Use known sound–letter patterns, useful word parts and recognised words, checking all printed letters. The suffix ed in planted forms a past action; do not call every frequent word irregular. Phrase practice can group “After lunch” / “the children carried a seed box” / “to the garden”, with other sensible groupings accepted. Controlled adult slip: read “The children planted six seats” while the child sees the actual seeds sentence. Notice seats/seeds mismatch, inspect the letters, repair to seeds and reread for meaning. A prompted repair is recorded separately from a spontaneous self-correction during ordinary reading.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.

html:
Complete story, fact and direction material

Story title: Seeds for the garden. “Nell packed a seed envelope for a train trip. At the station she checked the platform sign. She arrived near the garden just as rain began. Nell put the envelope under her coat and waited under a shelter. When the rain stopped, she planted the seeds.” Before reading, predict possible topic words such as station or garden, then check which actually occur. Literal: Nell waits under a shelter. Inference: keeping the envelope under her coat may protect it from rain; this is supported, not a quoted reason. Visualise the stated place and actions without treating imagined colours as facts. Summary: Nell travels with seeds, waits for the rain to stop, then plants them. Sequence cards: packed seeds / reached rainy garden / waited / planted. Fact card: “Our class planted six seeds on Monday. Four shoots were visible on Friday.” Listen for the stated numbers and days; do not infer that the other seeds can never grow. Directions: draw a rectangle, write Garden inside it, then put a star above it. Listen and follow the actual sequence, ask about an unclear word, and check the finished response. A relevant connection helps understanding; a personal story should not replace the text clues.
reason: Supply complete actual in-section stimuli/material protocol for the retained tasks.
